fields.title: Zones, Regions, and What They Protect Against
fields.keyTakeaway: Multi-zone setups protect against data center failure cheaply, multi-region setups are needed for legal and geographical reasons rather than reliability, and neither protects against logic errors.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: "Deploy in two regions" — what does this protect against and what does it not?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Multi-region setup is the most expensive reliability measure and the most frequently proposed without analysis. It protects against a narrow class of events and makes everything else more expensive — every change, every migration, every incident.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Single server.** Hardware failure causes downtime until recovery. **Multiple [[availability-zone|availability zones]] in a single region.** Different data centers connected by a fast network. Protects against individual center failure. Inter-zone latency is single-digit milliseconds, synchronous replication is possible. Moderate cost. **Multiple [[region|regions]].** Different geographies. Protects against regional events and solves [[data-residency|data residency]] and user proximity requirements. Inter-region latency is tens or hundreds of milliseconds, synchronous replication is impractical.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: The key distinction for the product: **data can be kept consistent between zones, but practically not between regions.** Hence all the complexities of multi-region setups.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **[[active-passive|Active-passive]].** One region works, the second is in reserve. Simpler, [[failover|failover]] takes minutes, unreplicated data is lost during switchover. **[[active-active|Active-active]].** Both serve traffic. Faster for users, but requires deciding what to do upon write conflicts and creates the risk of [[split-brain|split-brain]] — both sites think they are primary and diverge.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: Split-brain is the worst-case scenario: data diverges and cannot be reconciled automatically. This is exactly why active-active is rarely justified for transactional data.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: Three honest reasons to go multi-region: legal data residency, latency for geographically distant users, and enterprise customer requirements. Reliability is the fourth and usually the weakest reason, because multi-zone is enough.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Three zones in one region. Zone failure is survived automatically, downtime is about two minutes for database switchover.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: A second region was discussed twice. The first time under the banner of reliability: we calculated it using `SC3-N1-L2` and abandoned it, as it is orders of magnitude off from paying off. The second time for residency for the Domashny chain: there it was not reliability, but a legal requirement, and the decision was made, but in the form of a separate installation rather than active-active.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: The distinction turned out to be crucial. A separate installation for one client takes six weeks. True multi-region with consistent data takes a quarter and brings constant complexity.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Multi-region does not protect against logic errors: data deleted by mistake will be deleted everywhere, a broken release will roll out everywhere. Backups and progressive rollouts protect against this, not geography.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Multi-zone setups protect against data center failure cheaply, multi-region setups are needed for legal and geographical reasons rather than reliability, and neither protects against logic errors.
